title: Masked Language Modeling (Encoder-Only)
oneLineScope: Encoder-only, bidirectional context: BERT and the masked-token objective that treats language understanding as a fill-in-the-blank problem.
prose:
The autoregressive factorization is the natural way to model sequences you generate token by token — the probability of each word given its left context. But for many tasks what you want is a representation of a complete utterance that can see both left and right context simultaneously: what does bank mean in this sentence? which noun does they refer to? what is the sentiment of this review? For those tasks, conditioning only on the left half of the context is a handicap, not a feature. The encoder-only transformer, trained with a masked language modeling objective, is the architecture that takes bidirectionality seriously.

Full bidirectional self-attention

Recall from the the-full-transformer node that the original encoder uses self-attention with no causal mask: every position's query can attend to every other position's key. The \(n \times n\) score matrix is fully populated; there is no above-diagonal zero-out. This bidirectional full self-attention is the defining structural difference from the decoder-only model. The residual stream is still \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per token position, flowing through \(L\) identical encoder blocks each containing a full self-attention sublayer and a position-wise FFN, both wrapped in residual and layer normalization. The output is a sequence of contextualized representations, one per token, each informed by the entire sequence simultaneously.

Why can't you simply train this bidirectional architecture as a next-token LM? With full bidirectional attention, the representation of token \(t\) already has access to tokens \(t+1, t+2, \ldots\) — so predicting \(x_t\) from the final-layer representation of position \(t\) is trivial: the answer is sitting in the representation. You would not be modeling language; you would be copying. A different training objective is needed, one that creates a genuine prediction problem while retaining bidirectionality.

The masked LM objective

Devlin et al. (2019) — BERT — solve this with a cloze-style task (a term linguists will recognize from the readability literature). Before a training sequence is fed to the model, a subset of its positions is selected at random — approximately 15% — and the model must predict the original token at those positions from context. This is the masked language modeling (MLM) objective. The loss is cross-entropy over the masked positions only:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid \tilde{x}_1, \ldots, \tilde{x}_n), \]

where \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of masked position indices and \(\tilde{x}\) is the corrupted sequence fed to the encoder. The unmasked positions contribute no loss — their representations are updated by gradient only through the masked positions' predictions, via backpropagation through the attention layers.

The 80/10/10 corruption rule is a deliberate design choice, not an arbitrary hyperparameter. Of the 15% selected positions: 80% are replaced with a special [MASK] token; 10% are replaced with a randomly chosen vocabulary token; and 10% are left as the original token. The reason for the mixture is train–test mismatch. At fine-tuning and inference time, the model sees real text — no [MASK] tokens appear in a sentiment classification input. If every masked position were replaced with [MASK] during pre-training, the model would learn to treat [MASK] as a special signal and might not develop useful representations for ordinary tokens. The 10% random substitution forces the model to maintain a skeptical, context-checking representation of every token position — it can never be entirely sure any token is genuine — which tends to produce richer contextual representations. The 10% unchanged positions provide a small but useful anchor. The math: only 1.5% of all tokens (10% of 15%) are randomly replaced, so the language modeling signal is barely diluted.

Special tokens: [CLS] and [SEP]

BERT prepends a [CLS] token (for "classification") to every input sequence. Because every position attends to every other, the final-layer representation of [CLS] accumulates information from the whole sequence; it is used as the aggregate sequence representation for classification tasks (sentiment, entailment). A [SEP] token is appended at the end of each sentence segment, allowing the model to process pairs of sentences — premise and hypothesis, question and passage — as a single packed sequence while still being able to distinguish boundaries.

Next-Sentence Prediction

BERT was pre-trained with a second auxiliary objective, next-sentence prediction (NSP): given two consecutive segments \(A\) and \(B\), predict (from the [CLS] representation) whether \(B\) genuinely followed \(A\) in the source corpus (positive) or is a randomly sampled segment (negative). The motivation was to give the model discourse-level coherence signal for tasks like question answering and natural language inference where the relationship between two sentences is the point. However, the honest account, disclosed by Liu et al. (2019) in RoBERTa, is that NSP appears to have been largely unhelpful: models trained without NSP, on more data with larger batches, consistently outperformed BERT on downstream benchmarks. RoBERTa's reanalysis suggested that the NSP loss was too easy (sentence boundaries are strong cues) and that BERT's original training was significantly under-optimized relative to what the data and compute could support. NSP is documented here because it was an architectural component of the original BERT and because the RoBERTa correction is the kind of honest empirical revisionism the field needs more of.

BERT configurations

Devlin et al. released two model sizes. BERT-base: \(L = 12\) encoder layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\), \(h = 12\) attention heads, ~110 million parameters. BERT-large: \(L = 24\) encoder layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 1024\), \(h = 16\) attention heads, ~340 million parameters. Both were pre-trained on BooksCorpus (~800M words) and English Wikipedia (~2.5B words), using WordPiece subword tokenization with a 30,000-token vocabulary. Training BERT-large required 64 TPU v2 chips for four days — a scale that was exceptional in 2018 and that RoBERTa (2019) already found was insufficiently long for the dataset size.

What encoder-only models do well and what they cannot

The bidirectional representations BERT produces are excellent for tasks where the answer is a function of a complete, fixed input: sentiment classification (the [CLS] vector), named-entity recognition (the per-token vectors), reading comprehension / extractive QA (the token vectors identify span boundaries). These are all understanding tasks — mapping input to a label or a selected span — and the encoder's full-context representations compress the information needed. What an encoder-only model cannot do is generate new sequences autoregressively: because every position sees the full sequence, there is no well-defined next-token probability to decode from (or rather, you would have to mask positions during inference, destroying the bidirectionality that is the architecture's whole point). For generation tasks — summarization, translation, open-ended text production — you need either a decoder-only model or the encoder-decoder combination; the encoder-decoder-contrast node maps out those tradeoffs directly.

A sequence with a [CLS] token at the start, a [MASK] token mid-sequence, and a [SEP] token at the end feeds into an embedding plus positional encoding layer, then through L encoder blocks each with full bidirectional self-attention and an FFN. diagrams.caption: Bidirectional fill-in-the-blank versus left-to-right prediction: the contrast in context regimes between masked LM and autoregressive LM.
diagrams.altText: Two panels side by side. Left panel labeled 'Masked LM (encoder-only)': a sentence with one token blanked out, arrows coming from both left and right neighbors converging on the blank, with the label 'predict from full context'. Right panel labeled 'Autoregressive LM (decoder-only)': a sentence with each token predicted only from the tokens to its left, shown as a one-directional left-to-right arrow chain, with the label 'predict from left context only'.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual side-by-side illustration contrasting two context regimes. Left panel, labeled 'Masked LM (encoder-only)': a short sentence such as 'The [MASK] sat on the mat.' where [MASK] is highlighted. Arrows flow in from both the left tokens and the right tokens, converging on [MASK], labeled 'full bidirectional context'. A note below reads 'every position sees every other'. Right panel, labeled 'Autoregressive LM (decoder-only)': the same sentence without masking, but each token has an arrow arriving only from the left side — a left-to-right chain. The rightmost position shows 'predict next token', and a note below reads 'each position sees only its past'. Emphasize the directional difference between the two panels. No tensor shapes needed; this is the conceptual intuition diagram.

bibliography.citation: Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding." NAACL-HLT. arXiv:1810.04805.
bibliography.annotation: The defining BERT paper. §3.1 specifies the encoder-only architecture and the two pre-training objectives (MLM and NSP); §3.3 gives the 80/10/10 corruption rationale; Appendix A lists the BERT-base and BERT-large hyperparameters. The primary authority for all numbers cited in this node.

bibliography.citation: Liu, Y., Ott, M., Goyal, N., Du, J., Joshi, M., Chen, D., Levy, O., Lewis, M., Zettlemoyer, L., & Stoyanov, V. (2019). "RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach." arXiv:1907.11692.
bibliography.annotation: The systematic ablation study that found NSP largely unnecessary and BERT significantly undertrained. §4 ablates the NSP objective and larger batch / more data training. Essential for the honest account of what BERT actually showed versus what was claimed.

bibliography.citation: Alammar, J. "The Illustrated BERT, ELMo, and co."
bibliography.annotation: Clear visual walkthrough of the BERT architecture, the masked-token objective, the [CLS]/[SEP] tokens, and how the pre-trained model is adapted to downstream tasks. The best starting point for seeing the ideas before reading the paper.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J.H. Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), Chapter 11: "Fine-Tuning and Masked Language Models."
bibliography.annotation: A textbook treatment that situates BERT within the broader NLP landscape, covering pre-training objectives, fine-tuning, span-based and classification tasks. Useful for the reader who wants the full didactic context around the BERT family, not just the paper.
